source.title: CodeAttack: Revealing Safety Generalization Challenges of Large Language Models via Code Completion
source.authors: Qi-Bing Ren; Chang Gao; Jing Shao; Jun-Chi Yan; Xin Tan; Yu Qiao; Wai Lam; Li-Zhuang Ma

record.tranche_reason: Tests safety generalization in a new setting—code-formatted harmful user requests—and reports harmful-completion rates. It does not test the fine-tuning, token-position, opening-token, or parameter-localization versions listed.
record.gate_note: The reported CodeAttack ASRs and ablations measure harmful responses to harmful user requests, so they are recorded as findings about code-domain safety generalization under fits_no_version. The paper does not test fine-tuning on harmful or benign data, per-token KL, compliant response prefills, suffixes or decoding changes as such, localized safety weights, or deepening training. Table 1 baseline-attack results are reported from another study and are not included. Rows from Tables 2–4 report the CodeAttack ablations and language comparison.
record.test_reason: CodeAttack turns harmful user queries into code-completion prompts and reports ASR. That is an input-side mismatched-generalization jailbreak, a related but different construct. It does no harmful or benign fine-tuning (V1/V2) and no per-token KL (V3). It uses no compliant-response prefill, suffix or decoding change (V4), no weight localization (V5), no test of why safety is shallow (V6) and no deepening training (V7). Qi et al. (an original) is cited only as the source of the GPT-4 judge, so the reader's 'tests/T3' is wrong. The findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also hypothesise that code training creates a misaligned bias that prioritizes code completion over safety, supported by the benign-snippet result. They add that stronger models self-evaluate harmfulness better, suggesting self-evaluation as a mitigation.
record.recipe_differences: CodeAttack reformulates harmful user queries as code-completion prompts; it does not fine-tune models or measure response-token KL. The paper reports that Python-to-C++/Go conversions were done automatically by GPT-4.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported ASR changes with input encoding (string, queue, stack), task-understanding method, output-specification method, and programming language. The text says stack prompts can reduce ASR for some smaller models; language and ablation results also vary by model.

fits_no_version.finding: Code-formatted harmful queries elicit harmful completions. The best encoding per model gives 80–94% ASR, varying strongly by encoding and model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Natural-language safety training generalizes poorly to harmful requests posed as code completion.

fits_no_version.finding: Less common programming languages raise ASR for some models, e.g. Claude-2 rises from 24% in Python to 74% in Go.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety generalization to code inputs degrades for less popular programming languages.

fits_no_version.finding: decode()-based task extraction and list-based output specification raise ASR over comment-only variants.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompts closer to the code distribution bypass safety more often.

fits_no_version.finding: Prepending benign quick-sort code raises CodeAttack ASR: GPT-4-1106 32→42%, Claude-2 36→54% (Table 5). Post hoc defenses barely reduce ASR except on GPT-4-1106 (Table 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A code-completion bias competes with safety; perturbation and paraphrase defenses do not stop code-based attacks.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (2024)
record.problems: The excerpt's narrative summary that CodeAttack succeeds more than 80% across all models conflicts with the individual ASRs printed in Table 1, which include lower values. The paper reports temperature 0 and a human/GPT-4 judge agreement study, but gives no uncertainty estimates for the ASRs. Some comparison results are taken from prior work and not directly run here.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 5 and 6 are omitted because the 60-row limit is reached by the individually reported Table 1–4 CodeAttack outcomes. Table 5 reports adding a benign quick-sort code snippet versus plain text for GPT-4-1106 and Claude-2; Table 6 reports CodeAttack ASRs under defense methods. Neither is a test of the listed versions.

untested.parts: No benign fine-tuning. The CodeLlama vs Llama-2-70b comparison is a different released model, not a controlled fine-tuning test.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding manipulation. The attack reformulates the user input only.
No test of the data or objective causing token-shallow safety. The authors hypothesise a code-training bias instead.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'problems' claim that the >80% statement conflicts with Table 1 is mistaken. The figure refers to each model's best encoding (min across models is GPT-4-0613 at 80% with stack), not every cell. Table 1 baseline-attack values come from Zeng et al. and were correctly excluded. The Table 1 header in the text extract is garbled, but the row values match the paper's column order.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-data fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign instruction-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
The paper tests code-formatted user inputs, not compliant response prefills, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes, or bypass by getting past initial response tokens.
No weight or rank localization test.
No test of whether safety-training data or objectives cause token-localized safety.
No training intended to deepen safety or test of whether deepening holds up.
